summary.text: 京 is an ancient graph interpreted as a tall built structure; an early script-style redraw shows a rooflike top, central opening, and long lower strokes. A high mound is another early explanation. Today 京 commonly means “capital,” but the evidence does not establish how that sense arose from the earlier ones.

formation.text: Treat 京 as a whole pictograph of a tall building or platform, as supported by paleographic interpretations. The graph is also explained as a high man-made mound in the Shuowen account. These are competing interpretations of its original referent; neither establishes a dated semantic path to “capital.”

components.text: 京 is analyzed here as one whole pictorial graph of a tall built form, not divided into modern-looking parts. Paleographic descriptions interpret early forms as a roof, tower, and wall; the oracle-style image is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact.

history.text: A modern vector redraw labeled as oracle-bone style has a broad rooflike top, central opening, and long lower strokes. It illustrates the building interpretation but is not a dated inscription or proof of the graph’s original meaning.

The paleographic database describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tall building and says the small-seal form simplified the tower element to 口. The available account supplies no dates for individual attestations, so it does not establish a fully dated sequence.

uncertainties.text: The evidence supports competing readings of the graph as a tall building or platform and as a high man-made mound. A separate proposal connects a hilltop shrine or settlement with “capital,” but the evidence does not establish that sequence. The route to the capital sense remains unresolved.
The cited sources do not date the earliest use of 京 for “capital” or demonstrate whether it developed from a mound or settlement sense, followed another path, or reflects a distinct word sense.

senses.text: The graph is interpreted as a tall building or platform; the Shuowen account instead explains 京 as a very high man-made mound. The available evidence does not resolve which interpretation best captures its earliest meaning.

senses.period: attested in a Tang poem by cited work; earliest use unresolved
senses.text: 京 has the sense “capital city”; a cited example occurs in Bai Juyi’s Tang poem, but this does not establish when the sense began or how it relates to the high-structure or mound meaning.
“Large” is recorded as a sense, but the gloss list does not establish its chronology or connection to the other meanings.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish a chronological semantic link between the high structure or mound interpretations and “capital” or “large.”

overview.text: 京 is interpreted as a picture of a tall building or high platform. It now commonly means “capital,” though the evidence does not show how that meaning developed from the earlier interpretations.

components.text: Read the graph as one picture of a tall built form; its visible parts are not treated as separate components here.
